claim: Human cells with extra chromosome engineered via microcell-mediated chromosome transfer often gain massive chromosomal rearrangements.
source: We show that human cells with extra chromosome engineered via microcell-mediated chromosome transfer often gain massive chromosomal rearrangements.
evidence: The manuscript presents data from SNP arrays and whole genome sequencing showing chromosomal rearrangements in cells created via MMCT.

claim: The rearrangements arose by chromosome shattering and rejoining as well as by replication-dependent mechanisms.
source: The rearrangements arose by chromosome shattering and rejoining as well as by replication-dependent mechanisms.
evidence: The manuscript presents breakpoint junction analysis showing microhomology and templated insertions indicative of both mechanisms.

claim: The isolated micronuclei lack functional lamin B1.
source: We show that the isolated micronuclei lack functional lamin B1 and become prone to envelope rupture, which leads to DNA damage and aberrant replication.
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shows 42% of micronuclei after mitotic slippage lack lamin B1 staining.

claim: Micronuclei lacking lamin B1 become prone to envelope rupture.
source: We show that the isolated micronuclei lack functional lamin B1 and become prone to envelope rupture, which leads to DNA damage and aberrant replication.
evidence: Data shows colocalization of nuclear and cytoplasmic markers in micronuclei lacking lamin B1, indicating envelope rupture.

claim: Envelope rupture in micronuclei leads to DNA damage.
source: We show that the isolated micronuclei lack functional lamin B1 and become prone to envelope rupture, which leads to DNA damage and aberrant replication.
evidence: TUNEL and γ-H2A.x assays show DNA damage is significantly higher in micronuclei with envelope rupture.

claim: The presence of functional lamin B1 partly correlates with micronuclei size.
source: The presence of functional lamin B1 partly correlates with micronuclei size, suggesting that the proper assembly of nuclear envelope might be sensitive to membrane curvature.
evidence: Measurements show lamin B1 positive micronuclei have average diameter of 2.7 μm while lamin B1 negative have 1.9 μm.

claim: Proper assembly of nuclear envelope might be sensitive to membrane curvature.
source: The presence of functional lamin B1 partly correlates with micronuclei size, suggesting that the proper assembly of nuclear envelope might be sensitive to membrane curvature.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the correlation between micronuclei size and lamin B1 presence.

claim: The chromosomal rearrangements in trisomic cells provide growth advantage compared to cells without rearrangements.
source: The chromosomal rearrangements in trisomic cells provide growth advantage compared to cells without rearrangements.
evidence: Soft agar colony formation assays show cell lines with rearranged chromosomes form more colonies than those with intact extra chromosomes.

claim: In HCT116-derived trisomic and tetrasomic cell lines, 201 CNAs were detected, of which 25 were found also in the parental HCT116 and 176 CNAs were found only in trisomic and tetrasomic cell lines.
source: In HCT116-derived trisomic and tetrasomic cell lines, we detected 201 CNAs, of which 25 were found also in the parental HCT116 and 176 CNAs were found only in trisomic and tetrasomic cell lines (Figure 1a).
evidence: SNP array and SMASH sequencing data quantified CNAs across cell lines.

claim: 139 unique copy number changes were determined in 29 of the 38 analyzed aneuploid HCT116-derived cell lines.
source: While 36 of these CNAs were shared among two or more cell lines, we determined a total of 139 unique copy number changes, 58 losses and 81 gains, in 29 of the 38 analyzed aneuploid cell lines.
evidence: Analysis of SNP array and SMASH data identified unique CNAs.

claim: 41% of unique CNAs affected only the aneuploid chromosome.
source: We noted that the identified unique CNAs were not evenly distributed throughout the genome. Instead, a significant part (41%, 71/172) of these unique CNAs affected only the aneuploid chromosome, while the disomic chromosomes carried on average only 2.5 CNAs per chromosome (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Statistical analysis of CNA distribution across chromosomes.

claim: CNAs affecting the transferred chromosome were significantly larger than CNAs affecting all other chromosomes (median size 15.8 Mb and 3.3 Mb, respectively).
source: Furthermore, CNAs affecting the transferred chromosome were significantly larger than CNAs affecting all other chromosomes (median size 15.8 Mb and 3.3 Mb, respectively, Figure 1b).
evidence: Statistical comparison of CNA sizes shows significant difference (t-test, p=1.3E-14).

claim: 97.3% of the CNAs specifically affected the transferred chromosome in seven clones analyzed by BAF.
source: 97.3% of the CNAs specifically affected the transferred chromosome in seven clones (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: B allele frequency analysis of phase-informative SNPs determined which chromosome was affected.

claim: 93.6% of tested breakpoint junctions were successfully validated by PCR.
source: To experimentally validate the breakpoint junctions, we designed primers and successfully obtained a PCR product for 93.6% tested breakpoint junctions (88/94).
evidence: PCR validation experiments confirmed breakpoint junctions.

claim: 97.7% of the breakpoint junctions were exclusively present in the respective tri- or tetrasomic clonal cell lines and not in the A9 donors.
source: PCR assays on control samples (A9 and parental HCT116) confirmed that 97.7% of the breakpoint junctions were exclusively present in the respective tri- or tetrasomic clonal cell lines and not in the A9 donors, which indicated that they occurred de novo.
evidence: PCR validation on control samples showed breakpoints are specific to aneuploid lines.

claim: Each transferred chromosome was altered by 1 to 33 unique breakpoint junctions (>10 kb).
source: Each transferred chromosome was altered by 1 to 33 unique breakpoint junctions (>10 kb), thus indicating a wide range of complexity in genomic rearrangements among the eight analyzed clones (Figure 1d,e, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Whole genome sequencing identified varying numbers of breakpoint junctions.

claim: Five of the eight sequenced HCT116 cell lines showed a complex pattern of rearrangements, comprising multiple breakpoint-junctions and frequent copy number oscillations.
source: Five of the eight sequenced HCT116 cell lines (Hte5-01, Htr8-05, Htr13-03, Htr18-02 and Htr21-03) showed a complex pattern of rearrangements, comprising multiple breakpoint-junctions and frequent copy number oscillations (Figure 1e, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Whole genome sequencing data shows complex rearrangement patterns.

claim: Examination of the breakpoint junctions revealed all four types of orientations (tail-head, head-tail, tail-tail and head-head).
source: Indeed, examination of the breakpoint junctions revealed all four types of orientations (tail-head, head-tail, tail-tail and head-head), as would be expected for chromothripsis (Figure 1f).
evidence: Breakpoint junction analysis identified all four orientation types.

claim: There is a predominance of microhomologous repair at the breakpoint junctions of the complex rearrangement.
source: Moreover, we determined a predominance of microhomologous repair at the breakpoint junctions of the complex rearrangement (Figure 1g).
evidence: Sanger sequencing of breakpoint junctions revealed microhomology patterns.

claim: Very short genomic segments ranging in size from 63 to 162 bp were retained in the affected chromosomes following rearrangement formation.
source: We detected nine of these short fragments, ranging in size from 63 to 162 bp.
evidence: Breakpoint junction sequencing identified short templated sequences.

claim: 49.3% of isolated micronuclei showed a comet structure in the comet assay.
source: In contrast, 49.3% of isolated MN showed a comet structure (Figure 2h,i).
evidence: Comet assay quantification of isolated micronuclei.

claim: A9 cells treated with colchicine for 48 hr showed similarly low frequency of comets as untreated cells.
source: We found that the mitotic slippage did not lead to additional DNA damage, as A9 cells treated with colchicine for 48 hr showed similarly low frequency of comets as untreated cells.
evidence: Comet assay comparison between treated and untreated cells.

claim: There was a significant increase of TUNEL-positive isolated micronuclei compared to donor cells.
source: While the donor cells showed only a low level of DNA damage even upon prolonged colchicine and cytochalasin B (DCB) treatment, there was a significant increase of TUNEL-positive isolated MN (Figure 2j,k).
evidence: TUNEL assay quantification shows significant difference (t-test, p<0.005).

claim: The average intensity of DAPI staining was significantly lower in the TUNEL-positive micronuclei than in the TUNEL-negative micronuclei.
source: Moreover, the average intensity of DAPI staining, a proxy for DNA content, was significantly lower in the TUNEL-positive micronuclei than in the TUNEL-negative micronuclei, suggesting either extensive DNA damage or loss through damaged envelope (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: DAPI intensity measurements compared between TUNEL-positive and negative micronuclei (t-test, p=0.0001).

claim: Colocalization of NLS with CLS was observed in 14% of isolated micronuclei.
source: In contrast, we observed colocalization of NLS with CLS in 14% of MNs, while NLS alone was detected only in 2% of the isolated MNs (Figure 3c).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy quantification of marker protein localization.

claim: The DAPI signal intensity was 3.6 times lower in micronuclei where both NLS and CLS signals colocalized than in all other micronuclei.
source: Additionally, the DAPI signal intensity was 3.6 times lower in MNs where both NLS and CLS signals colocalized than in all other MNs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: DAPI intensity measurements in micronuclei with different marker patterns.

claim: Lamin B1 staining was absent in 42% of micronuclei after mitotic slippage.
source: In contrast, lamin B1 staining was present in all primary nuclei, but absent in 42% of MN after mitotic slippage (Figure 3d,e).
evidence: Immunofluorescence quantification of lamin B1 in micronuclei.

claim: The procedure of micronuclei isolation did not affect lamin B1 localization to the nuclear envelope.
source: The procedure of MN isolation did not affect lamin B1 localization to the NE, since comparable fraction of MN after isolation lacked lamin B1 (49%) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Comparison of lamin B1 presence before and after isolation shows similar percentages.

claim: The average diameter of lamin B1 positive micronuclei was 2.7 μm, while the average diameter of lamin B1 negative micronuclei was 1.9 μm.
source: We noticed that the presence of lamin B1 correlates with the size of the micronucleus: while the average diameter of lamin B1 positive micronuclei was 2.7 μm, the average diameter of lamin B1 negative micronuclei was 1.9 μm (Figure 3f).
evidence: Diameter measurements of micronuclei with and without lamin B1 (Mann Whitney test, p=0.00012).

claim: Spontaneously arising micronuclei in RPE1 cells showed a similar correlation between lamin B1 presence and size.
source: The correlation appears to be a general feature, since spontaneously arising micronuclei in RPE1 cells showed a similar trend (Figure 3g).
evidence: Diameter measurements in RPE1 micronuclei show similar pattern (Mann Whitney test, p<0.0001).

claim: DNA damage can be detected in nearly 80% of lamin B1-negative micronuclei.
source: Indeed, co-staining of MNs with lamin B1 antibody and TUNEL assay showed that DNA damage can be detected in nearly 80% of lamin B1-negative micronuclei, while only 20% of lamin B1-positive micronuclei showed TUNEL signal (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: Co-staining experiments quantified TUNEL positivity in relation to lamin B1 status.

claim: Only 20% of lamin B1-positive micronuclei showed TUNEL signal.
source: Indeed, co-staining of MNs with lamin B1 antibody and TUNEL assay showed that DNA damage can be detected in nearly 80% of lamin B1-negative micronuclei, while only 20% of lamin B1-positive micronuclei showed TUNEL signal (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: Co-staining experiments quantified TUNEL positivity in relation to lamin B1 status.

claim: The occurrence of TUNEL positive micronuclei decreased by 60% when microcells were isolated at 4°C.
source: The occurrence of TUNEL positive micronuclei decreased by 60% when we isolated the microcells at 4°C. (Figure 4c), suggesting that the DNA damage arises through enzymatic activity, most probably of cytoplasmic nucleases.
evidence: Comparison of TUNEL positivity at different isolation temperatures.

claim: DNA damage arises through enzymatic activity, most probably of cytoplasmic nucleases.
source: The occurrence of TUNEL positive micronuclei decreased by 60% when we isolated the microcells at 4°C. (Figure 4c), suggesting that the DNA damage arises through enzymatic activity, most probably of cytoplasmic nucleases.
evidence: Temperature-dependent reduction in DNA damage suggests enzymatic mechanism.

claim: Nearly 50% of lamin B1-negative micronuclei showed γ-H2A.x signal.
source: Additionally, DNA damage was detected in nearly 50% of lamin B1-negative micronuclei, while only 22.5% of lamin B1-positive micronuclei showed γ-H2A.x signal (Figure 4f).
evidence: Immunofluorescence quantification of γ-H2A.x in relation to lamin B1 status.

claim: Only 22.5% of lamin B1-positive micronuclei showed γ-H2A.x signal.
source: Additionally, DNA damage was detected in nearly 50% of lamin B1-negative micronuclei, while only 22.5% of lamin B1-positive micronuclei showed γ-H2A.x signal (Figure 4f).
evidence: Immunofluorescence quantification of γ-H2A.x in relation to lamin B1 status.

claim: DNA damage (γ-H2A.x signal) was identified in 58% of micronuclei with nuclear localization of CLS.
source: Finally, DNA damage (γ-H2A.x signal) was identified in 58% of MNs with nuclear localization of CLS, while less than 20% of MNs without nuclear CLS showed DNA damage (Figure 4g).
evidence: Quantification of γ-H2A.x in micronuclei with and without CLS signal (p=0.0036).

claim: Less than 20% of micronuclei without nuclear CLS showed DNA damage.
source: Finally, DNA damage (γ-H2A.x signal) was identified in 58% of MNs with nuclear localization of CLS, while less than 20% of MNs without nuclear CLS showed DNA damage (Figure 4g).
evidence: Quantification of γ-H2A.x in micronuclei with and without CLS signal (p=0.0036).

claim: Micronuclei from samples that underwent centrifugation steps showed elevated γ-H2A.x signal.
source: Importantly, the MN from samples that underwent centrifugation steps showed elevated γ-H2A.x signal (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Comparison of γ-H2A.x signal with and without centrifugation.

claim: Cell lines with a rearranged chromosome formed colonies in soft agar more readily than the cell lines with an identical, but intact chromosome.
source: Strikingly, we found that the cell lines with a rearranged chromosome formed colonies in soft agar more readily than the cell lines with an identical, but intact chromosome (Figure 5a,b).
evidence: Soft agar colony formation assays comparing rearranged vs intact chromosomes.

claim: The accumulation of anaphase bridges and micronuclei negatively correlates with the colony formation.
source: Strikingly, the accumulation of anaphase bridges and micronuclei negatively correlates with the colony formation, suggesting that increased genomic instability impairs cellular proliferation in soft agar (Figure 5d).
evidence: Correlation analysis between mitotic errors and colony formation (Spearman correlation, rs=-0.8667, p=0.0045).

claim: Increased genomic instability impairs cellular proliferation in soft agar.
source: Strikingly, the accumulation of anaphase bridges and micronuclei negatively correlates with the colony formation, suggesting that increased genomic instability impairs cellular proliferation in soft agar (Figure 5d).
evidence: Inference from negative correlation between genomic instability markers and colony formation.

claim: The less extra DNA the cells contain, the more colonies they form.
source: We therefore correlated the amount of extra DNA with the ability to form colonies on soft agar, demonstrating that the less extra DNA the cells contain, the more colonies they form (Figure 5e).
evidence: Correlation analysis between additional genomic material and colony formation (Spearman correlation, rs=-0.7275, p=0.0032).

claim: The occurrence of anaphase bridges and chromosome missegregation correlated with the amount of additional genomic material.
source: Interestingly, the occurrence of anaphase bridges and chromosome missegregation also correlated with the amount of additional genomic material (Figure 5f, Figure 5—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Correlation analysis between additional genomic material and anaphase bridges.

claim: Micronuclei are not only a consequence of chromosome instability, but further facilitate genomic aberrations.
source: Recent research suggests that micronuclei are not only a consequence of chromosome instability, but further facilitate genomic aberrations (Hatch and Hetzer, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Lamin B is lacking in 30–50% of micronuclei.
source: For example lamin B is lacking in 30–50% of micronuclei, which renders the micronuclei vulnerable to physical forces generated by actin cytoskeleton or during movements of cells through constricted areas, which may result in nuclear rupture (Hatch et al., 2013; Hatch and Hetzer, 2016; Irianto et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The nuclear envelope of micronuclei often lacks nuclear pores.
source: The NE of micronuclei often lacks other components, such as nuclear pores (Crasta et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chromosomes trapped in micronuclei are frequently underreplicated, or their replication occurs later than the replication in the primary nuclei.
source: Additionally, chromosomes trapped in micronuclei are frequently underreplicated, or their replication occurs later than the replication in the primary nuclei (Crasta et al., 2012; Okamoto et al., 2012; Soto et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chromothripsis is a frequent phenomenon in cancer genomes.
source: Chromothripsis, a frequent phenomenon in cancer genomes, enables cancer cells to generate rapid and massive changes in their chromosomal architecture by means of a one-off catastrophic event (Korbel and Campbell, 2013; Stephens et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chromothripsis enables cancer cells to generate rapid and massive changes in their chromosomal architecture by means of a one-off catastrophic event.
source: Chromothripsis, a frequent phenomenon in cancer genomes, enables cancer cells to generate rapid and massive changes in their chromosomal architecture by means of a one-off catastrophic event (Korbel and Campbell, 2013; Stephens et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chromothripsis breakpoints show blunt fusions or microhomology, indicating repair of fragmented chromosomes through non-homologous or microhomologous repair.
source: Chromothripsis breakpoints show blunt fusions or microhomology, indicating repair of fragmented chromosomes through non-homologous or microhomologous repair, suggesting that the rearrangements result from localized chromosome shattering by double-stranded DNA breaks, followed by random reassembly of chromosomal fragments (Kloosterman et al., 2011; Kloosterman et al., 2012; Morrison et al., 2014; Rausch et al., 2012; Stephens et al., 2011; Storchová and Kloosterman, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chromothripsis has been found in patients with congenital disorders and even in healthy individuals.
source: Chromothripsis has also been found in patients with congenital disorders and even in healthy individuals (Chiang et al., 2012; de Pagter et al., 2015; Kloosterman et al., 2012; Stephens et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Micronuclei containing chromosomes were recently pointed out as one of the routes towards chromothripsis-like rearrangements.
source: Micronuclei containing chromosomes were recently pointed out as one of the routes towards chromothripsis-like rearrangements, as chromosomes sequestered to micronuclei with abnormal NE become liable to aberrant DNA repair and replication, which may lead to massive chromosomal rearrangements (Crasta et al., 2012; Ly and Cleveland, 2017; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Microcell-mediated chromosome transfer is often used to construct cells with extra chromosomes to analyze the consequences of chromosome gain.
source: Microcell mediated chromosome transfer (MMCT) is often used to construct cells with extra chromosomes to analyze the consequences of chromosome gain (Fournier and Ruddle, 1977).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The transferred chromosome was incorporated into the primary nucleus 48 hr – 72 hr after the fusion.
source: The transferred chromosome was incorporated into the primary nucleus 48 hr – 72 hr after the fusion, which was documented by chromosome painting in the interphase (Figure 2g).
evidence: Chromosome painting experiments documented timing of incorporation.

claim: The replication of micronuclei was often asynchronous with the primary nucleus.
source: The replication of MN was often asynchronous with the primary nucleus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), supporting the notion that replication is dysfunctional in MNs.
evidence: EdU incorporation experiments showed asynchronous replication patterns.

claim: Trisomic cell lines derived from non-transformed RPE1 carry markedly less de novo rearrangements than HCT116-derived lines.
source: This was particularly prominent in HCT116-derived trisomic cell lines, where 66% of them showed more than one rearrangement on the transferred chromosome. Trisomic cell lines derived from non-transformed RPE1 carry markedly less de novo rearrangements (compare Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: Comparison of CNA data between HCT116 and RPE1 derived cell lines.

claim: 66% of HCT116-derived trisomic cell lines showed more than one rearrangement on the transferred chromosome.
source: This was particularly prominent in HCT116-derived trisomic cell lines, where 66% of them showed more than one rearrangement on the transferred chromosome.
evidence: Analysis of rearrangements across HCT116-derived cell lines.

claim: Non-transformed cells with fully functional checkpoints are less tolerant to DNA damage and aneuploidy than cancerous cells.
source: This might be due to the fact that the non-transformed cells with fully functional checkpoints are less tolerant to DNA damage and aneuploidy than cancerous cells.
evidence: This is an inference to explain the difference in rearrangement frequency between cell types.

claim: Micronuclei that arise from mitotic slippage in the absence of microtubules fail to properly localize lamin B1 to the nuclear envelope.
source: Taken together, we propose that micronuclei that arise from mitotic slippage in the absence of microtubules fail to properly localize lamin B1 to the NE.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental observations.

claim: A higher curvature of the nuclear envelope in micronuclei may negatively affect the lamina assembly.
source: We hypothesize that a higher curvature of the NE in MN may negatively affect the lamina assembly, similarly as it was demonstrated in primary nuclei where high membrane curvature impairs nuclear lamina (Denais et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on observations and cited previous work.

claim: Gain of a chromosome generally impairs cellular proliferation in human cells.
source: Gain of a chromosome generally impairs cellular proliferation in human cells and most trisomic human cells proliferate slower than their isogenic parental cell line (Sheltzer et al., 2017; Stingele et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Chromothripsis provides growth advantage also in near-diploid cells.
source: Here we demonstrate for the first time that chromothripsis provides growth advantage also in near-diploid cells.
evidence: Soft agar assays comparing near-diploid cells with and without chromothripsis.

claim: Chromosomal rearrangements reduce the negative effects of chromosome gain on cellular proliferation by reducing the amount of extra DNA.
source: Comparison of proliferation of cell lines carrying intact extra chromosomes with cell lines carrying rearranged chromosomes revealed that the chromosomal rearrangements reduce the negative effects of chromosome gain on cellular proliferation by reducing the amount of extra DNA (Figure 5).
evidence: Correlation analysis between extra DNA amount and colony formation ability.

claim: Increased genomic instability is an important factor that negatively affects proliferation of trisomic cells.
source: At the same time, our data reveal that increased genomic instability is an important factor that negatively affects proliferation of trisomic cells.
evidence: Correlation between mitotic errors and colony formation ability.

claim: Htr13-03 lost the extra copies of COL4A2 and COL4A1, while Htr13-02 carries three copies of each.
source: For example, individual assessment of the analyzed cell lines revealed that Htr13-03 (with rearranged chromosomes 13) lost the extra copies of COL4A2 and COL4A1, while Htr13-02 (with intact chromosome 13) carries three copies of each (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Copy number analysis of specific genes in cell lines.

claim: COL4A2 and COL4A1 encode type IV collagen alpha proteins.
source: COL4A2 and COL4A1 encode type IV collagen alpha proteins.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge about these genes.

claim: Upon proteolytic cleavage of COL4A2 and COL4A1, biologically active peptides called Arresten and Canstatin, respectively, are formed that inhibit angiogenesis, proliferation and tumor formation.
source: Upon proteolytic cleavage of COL4A2 and COL4A1, biologically active peptides called Arresten and Canstatin, respectively, are formed that inhibit angiogenesis, proliferation and tumor formation (Egeblad et al., 2010; Kamphaus et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Lamin A/C staining was present in nearly all primary nuclei and micronuclei.
source: Immunostaining analysis demonstrated that lamin A/C staining was present in nearly all primary nuclei and MN.
evidence: Immunofluorescence quantification of lamin A/C.

claim: Lamin B1 staining was present in all primary nuclei.
source: In contrast, lamin B1 staining was present in all primary nuclei, but absent in 42% of MN after mitotic slippage (Figure 3d,e).
evidence: Immunofluorescence quantification of lamin B1.

claim: The size of micronuclei correlates with the number of encapsulated chromosomes.
source: Evaluation of the chromosome number using centromeric antibody revealed that the size of MNs correlates with the number of encapsulated chromosomes.
evidence: Immunofluorescence analysis of centromeres and micronuclei size measurements.

claim: Micronuclei lacking lamin B were consistently smaller than micronuclei with lamin B regardless the chromosomal content.
source: Interestingly, MNs lacking lamin B were consistently smaller than MNs with lamin B regardless the chromosomal content (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Size measurements of micronuclei stratified by lamin B status and chromosome number.

claim: The lack of lamin B renders the micronuclei prone to further size reduction, possibly due to DNA damage and loss.
source: This observation might be explained by our finding that the lack of lamin B renders the MNs prone to further size reduction, possibly due to DNA damage and loss.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between lamin B absence and smaller size.

claim: A failure of small micronuclei to incorporate lamin B efficiently may contribute to the correlation between size and lamin B presence.
source: Additionally, a failure of small MNs to incorporate lamin B efficiently may also contribute to this effect.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed correlation.

claim: Micronuclei lacking lamin B1 often lose the nuclear envelope integrity.
source: This corroborated that MN lacking lamin B often loose the NE integrity, which was documented by the nuclear localization of CLS (Figure 4e).
evidence: Fluorescence microscopy showing CLS localization in lamin B1-negative micronuclei.

claim: Mechanical forces that arise during the isolation procedure may facilitate rupture of the micronuclei.
source: We propose that the mechanical forces that arise during the isolation procedure may also facilitate rupture of the MNs.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on comparison of DNA damage with and without centrifugation.

claim: DNA damage or replication-dependent rearrangements can occur in micronuclei after fusion to the acceptor cells.
source: Additionally, DNA damage or replication-dependent rearrangements can occur in MN after fusion to the acceptor cells, as suggested by the finding of patterns of aberrant replication processes on the rarranged chromosomes in trisomic cells (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the patterns of rearrangements observed in the sequencing data.

claim: Aurora B kinase activity affects assembly of the nuclear envelope around lagging chromosomes and interferes with efficient lamin B deposition via 'chromosome separation checkpoint'.
source: Previous works suggested that Aurora B kinase activity affects assembly of the NE around lagging chromosomes and interferes with efficient lamin B deposition via so called 'chromosome separation checkpoint' (Afonso et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Microtubuli of the mitotic spindle interfere with the proper assembly of nuclear envelope around lagging chromosomes in late stages of mitosis.
source: Alternatively, microtubuli of the mitotic spindle interfere with the proper assembly of NE around lagging chromosomes in late stages of mitosis (Liu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The micronuclei created in MMCT form during mitotic slippage due to a treatment with microtubule poison, which reduces the probability of the interference of microtubules with nuclear envelope assembly.
source: First, the micronuclei created in MMCT form during mitotic slippage due to a treatment with microtubule poison, which reduces the probability of the interference of microtubules with NE assembly.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the experimental design.

claim: The micronuclei arise after nuclear slippage, where no chromosome separation took place.
source: Second, the micronuclei arise after nuclear slippage, where no chromosome separation took place.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of micronuclei formation in the MMCT procedure.

claim: High membrane curvature impairs nuclear lamina in primary nuclei.
source: We hypothesize that a higher curvature of the NE in MN may negatively affect the lamina assembly, similarly as it was demonstrated in primary nuclei where high membrane curvature impairs nuclear lamina (Denais et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Chromothripsis improves cellular proliferation in soft agar in tetraploid background.
source: Previous work suggested that chromothripsis improves cellular proliferation in soft agar, however, it is important to note that the experiments were performed in tetraploid background (Mardin et al., 2015) and tetraploidy alone facilitates proliferation in soft agar (Fujiwara et al., 2005; Kuznetsova et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tetraploidy alone facilitates proliferation in soft agar.
source: Previous work suggested that chromothripsis improves cellular proliferation in soft agar, however, it is important to note that the experiments were performed in tetraploid background (Mardin et al., 2015) and tetraploidy alone facilitates proliferation in soft agar (Fujiwara et al., 2005; Kuznetsova et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: MMCT may serve as a model system for analysis of mechanisms involved in chromothripsis of specific chromosomes and their consequences.
source: Thus, we demonstrate that MMCT may serve as a model system for analysis of mechanisms involved in chromothripsis of specific chromosomes and their consequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented.

claim: MMCT is the only model system that allows targeted generation of chromothripsis of any chromosome in human cell lines.
source: Although MMCT is an artificial system to generate micronuclei, we note that this is to our knowledge the only model system that allows targeted generation of chromothripsis of any chromosome in human cell lines.
evidence: This is a claim about the uniqueness of the model system based on the authors' knowledge.

claim: The chromosomal rearrangements occurred on the specific chromosome entrapped in the micronuclei and used for the MMCT.
source: Secondly, we show that the chromosomal rearrangements occurred on the specific chromosome entrapped in the micronuclei and used for the MMCT.
evidence: BAF analysis and breakpoint validation showed rearrangements specifically affect the transferred chromosome.

claim: Both replication-based mechanisms and chromosome shattering followed by double-strand break repair occur during chromosome transfer and lead to stably maintained rearrangements.
source: Our data show that both replication-based mechanisms and chromosome shattering followed by double-strand break repair occur during chromosome transfer and lead to stably maintained rearrangements.
evidence: Breakpoint junction analysis revealed signatures of both mechanisms.

claim: The arising trisomic and tetrasomic cells further propagate despite chromothripsis.
source: The arising trisomic and tetrasomic cells further propagate despite chromothripsis.
evidence: Cell lines with chromothripsis were successfully established and maintained.

claim: The rearrangements were not identified in the donor cell lines before the transfer.
source: Importantly, these rearrangements were not identified in the donor cell lines before the transfer, thus supporting the idea that the passage through micronuclei contributed to their formation.
evidence: PCR validation showed breakpoints were not present in donor cells.

claim: Only one common CNA was identified on the transferred chromosome, suggesting its origin in the common donor.
source: (1) Only one common CNA was identified on the transferred chromosome, suggesting its origin in the common donor (Figure 1a).
evidence: Analysis of CNAs across cell lines identified shared aberrations.

claim: PCR over the breakpoint junctions did not reveal their presence in the donor cell lines.
source: (2) PCR over the breakpoint junctions did not reveal their presence in the donor cell lines (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: PCR validation experiments on donor cells.

claim: The rearrangement formation within micronuclei during MMCT may result from aberrant replicative processes (serial template switching) as well as from chromosome shattering by double-strand breaks, followed by DNA repair.
source: On the basis of the genomic hallmarks of the induced rearrangements, we propose that the rearrangement formation within micronuclei during MMCT may result from aberrant replicative processes (serial template switching) as well as from chromosome shattering by double-strand breaks, followed by DNA repair (Kloosterman et al., 2012; Stephens et al., 2011; Holland and Cleveland, 2012; Liu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on breakpoint characteristics and cited previous work.

claim: Removal of unnecessary genetic material is a previously unappreciated effect of chromosomal rearrangements.
source: This is on one hand due to a previously unappreciated effect of chromosomal rearrangements, which is a removal of unnecessary genetic material, and we propose that this aspect may be another important factor that shapes cancer genomes.
evidence: This is a novel interpretation of the functional consequences of rearrangements based on the data.
